blocks.text: …the president of the tenants' cooperative that legally owns this building."

I sat down on an old filing cabinet. My mother lived in this building from 1990 until 2008, when I was twenty-five. She died in 2015. She'd always called it "our building," and I'd always thought she was just being sentimental.

The inspector, Mr. Boyd, spent the next two hours going through the files with me. In 1994, the building's elderly owner died with no heirs. His will left the property to its tenants as a cooperative, on one condition: it had to remain affordable housing. The tenants elected my mother president. She organized the paperwork, collected the rent, and applied for a city housing assistance program to help pay for repairs. The program issued checks to the cooperative every year.
Then, in 1995, a property manager named Victor Gale offered to "help" the cooperative with its finances.

Within a year, he'd filed paperwork with the county claiming the co-op had sold him the building. The signatures were forged. My mother fought it, but she couldn't afford a lawyer, and the county records office accepted his documents. Gale took over the building and raised the rents. He couldn't cash the assistance checks, which were made out to the cooperative, so he hid them, along with every record that proved the co-op existed. He built a wall in the basement to keep them out of sight.
My mother spent the rest of her life believing she'd failed her neighbors.
The city attorney's office opened a fraud investigation that week. A handwriting expert confirmed the 1995 transfer documents were forged.
Because the original owner's will required the building to stay in the cooperative, a judge ruled that Gale's ownership claim was invalid.

The building now belongs to its tenants again, as it always should have. Some of the residents who lived without proper heat had been there since my mother's time. Mrs. Delgado, who is eighty-one, cried when she heard. She said, "Your mother told us we'd win someday. We just thought she meant in heaven."
The uncashed checks were reissued by the city, with interest, to the cooperative. That money is paying for a new boiler and a new roof.
At our first co-op meeting, the tenants elected a new president. I told them they were making a mistake. They told me I'd already fixed the lights.
My rent didn't go up $1,200. It went down $300. My mother's photograph hangs in the lobby now, next to the original 1994 deed with her signature on it.
